segments.text: Note on sourcing: the concepts, frameworks, and named models in this chapter (Fayol’s functions, Mintzberg’s roles, Katz’s skills, Porter’s generic strategies, Maslow’s hierarchy, Herzberg’s two-factor theory, Vroom’s expectancy theory, Lewin’s change model, CAPM, WACC, EOQ, and the bullwhip effect) are long-established, widely taught frameworks covered in the standard textbooks listed above. Numerical examples in this chapter are illustrative worked calculations constructed to demonstrate the underlying formulas, not reported findings from a specific study. # Public Administration
CSS/PMS Group III Optional Subject — Code 23, 100 marks

Public Administration is the study of how government institutions are organized, staffed, financed, and controlled so that laws and public policies are actually turned into real services for citizens. It differs from private management in one crucial respect: every administrative act operates inside a web of constitutional, legal, political, and public-accountability constraints that a private firm does not face in the same way — a public manager cannot simply decide to serve a profitable segment of customers and ignore the rest, because public service carries obligations of universality, legality, and fairness that private management does not.

The subject is organized into twelve connected units: the first two build the conceptual and theoretical vocabulary (what public administration is, and the major theories used to understand administrative behaviour); the middle units cover the practical machinery of government (policy, budgeting, personnel, law, management skills, the civil service, and provincial/local government); and the final units cover how that machinery is reformed, held accountable, and connected to national development.

Robert B. Denhardt’s Public Administration, David H. Rosenbloom’s Public Administration: Understanding Management, Politics and Law, Nicholas Henry’s Public Administration and Public Affairs, Charles H. Kennedy’s Bureaucracy in Pakistan, and the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan (for institutional context) are the standard reference works behind this syllabus.
